239.title: The peacemakers (Matthew 5:9)
239.hook: peacemakers, not peacekeepers: they make peace where there wasn't any
239.carry: make peace, not just keep it
239.howItsDone: Many churches share the peace in worship, turning to neighbors to say peace be with you, and Christians, especially in the historic peace churches, work at mediation and reconciliation between people and communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pure in heart, and your line was a single heart sees. What did you give your whole heart to? Day two hundred thirty-nine.

Every family has a peacekeeper. The one who changes the subject when politics comes up at dinner. Who says, let's not get into it. Who smooths things over so nobody storms out. It's a real gift, and often an exhausting one. But notice: under a kept peace, the problem is usually still there. The two brothers still aren't speaking. The old hurt is still sitting in the corner. The seventh line of the sermon doesn't bless the peacekeepers. It uses a different word.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY HAS A PEACEKEEPER.` → `LET'S NOT GET INTO IT.` → `A DIFFERENT WORD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." The Greek word is eirenopoioi. Eirene is peace; poieo is to make, to build, the root of our word poem. Peace-makers. People who build a peace that wasn't there before. It's the only time this word appears in the whole New Testament. And the peace behind it is the Hebrew shalom. Shalom isn't just no fighting. It's wholeness: everything in its right place, nothing missing, nothing broken. So a peacemaker doesn't just stop the shouting. They go into the broken place and help build something whole. That's harder. It usually means naming what's wrong, listening to both sides, and taking some heat. Peacemakers often get shot at from both directions. Now think about the world Jesus said this in. Rome boasted of the Pax Romana, the Roman peace, a peace kept by legions and crosses. Jesus blesses a different kind: peace that's made, not enforced. And the promise: they shall be called the children of God. In Hebrew idiom, the son of something shares its character. Peacemakers are called God's children because they're doing what, Christians say, God does: making peace between people who were apart. Paul would later put the practical version this way: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men." If it be possible. As much as lieth in you. It takes two to make peace. But you can do your half.
screen: `EIRENE PLUS POIEO: PEACE-BUILDERS.` · `SHALOM: NOTHING MISSING, NOTHING BROKEN.` · `NOT ENFORCED, BUT MADE.` · `CALLED THE CHILDREN OF GOD.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one peace today. Settle, and breathe. Think of a relationship where there's a quiet cold war: not a battle, just a chill. Someone you avoid. Something unsaid. Picture that person. Then ask: what would be my half of making peace? Maybe it's an apology. Maybe it's asking, are we okay? Maybe it's just a friendly message after a long silence. Choose the smallest real step. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for courage. The bell holds the time.
The peacemakers. Eirenopoioi, peace builders: people who make shalom where there wasn't any, and are called the children of God.
Your line: make peace, not just keep it. Today, take the smallest real step toward one peace: one message, one question, one apology. Your half is enough. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

240.title: Persecuted (Matthew 5:10–12)
240.hook: blessed when you're insulted for doing right
240.howItsDone: Christians remember martyrs on their feast days, and many churches set aside a day or a Sunday each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the peacemakers: people who build peace where there wasn't any. Did you take one small step toward a peace? Day two hundred forty.

Think of the time you did the right thing and it cost you. You spoke up for someone and got frozen out of the group. You told the truth and lost the deal. You refused to laugh at the joke and became the next joke. Doing right doesn't always get applause. Sometimes it gets you punished. The last of the Beatitudes is the one nobody puts on a coffee mug. After the empty-handed, the mourners, the meek, the hungry, the merciful, the pure and the peacemakers, Jesus blesses the people who get hurt for it.
screen: `IT COST YOU.` → `THE NEXT JOKE.` → `THE LAST BEATITUDE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Listen to that ending. Theirs is the kingdom of heaven. It's the same promise as the very first beatitude, the poor in spirit. The list opens and closes with the same words, like bookends. Everything in between lives inside the kingdom. And notice: for righteousness' sake. Not for being difficult, or rude, or right in an annoying way. For doing what's right. Then Jesus turns and speaks straight to the people in front of him, not they any more but ye: blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. And then the strangest instruction in the sermon: "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you." The Greek word for be exceeding glad is agalliasthe. It's more than smiling through it. It's the word for jumping for joy. Why rejoice? Not because pain is good. Because you're in good company: the prophets walked this road before you. The book of Acts tells how the apostles, after being beaten, left rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer for his name. Christians have been persecuted in many times and places, from the first centuries to today, and people of many faiths know that suffering too. For many Christians, this beatitude has been less a theory and more a lifeline: whatever happens, it isn't the end, and you're not alone.
screen: `THE SAME PROMISE AS THE FIRST.` · `FOR RIGHTEOUSNESS' SAKE.` · `AGALLIASTHE: JUMP FOR JOY.` · `IN GOOD COMPANY: THE PROPHETS.` · then, large: `REJOICE, AND BE EXCEEDING GLAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember Christians who suffer for their faith today. Settle, and breathe. Around the world, some Christians face prison, violence or losing their homes for what they believe. Picture one of them: a pastor in a cell, a family that had to flee, a teenager mocked at school for praying. If you pray, you can pray for them now, by name if you know one. If you don't pray, simply hold them in mind, and wish them courage and safety. The bell holds the time.
Persecuted. The last beatitude: blessed are those hurt for doing right, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Your line: rejoice anyway. Today, if doing right costs you something small, notice it, and remember you're in good company. Day two hundred forty.

241.title: Salt and light (Matthew 5:13–16)
241.hook: you are the salt of the earth, the light of the world
241.howItsDone: At many baptisms a candle is lit and given to the newly baptized as a sign that they are to be light in the world, and Christians often use salt and light as pictures for living their faith in ordinary places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last beatitude, persecuted for doing right, and your line was rejoice anyway. Did doing right cost you anything small? Day two hundred forty-one.

She's the salt of the earth. People still say it about a grandmother, a neighbor, the guy at the hardware store: someone solid, honest, no fuss. Most people who say it have no idea they're quoting Jesus. Right after the Beatitudes, Jesus looks at the people in front of him, fishermen and farmers, nobody important, and tells them two things about who they are. Not who they should become someday. Who they already are.
screen: `SALT OF THE EARTH.` → `QUOTING JESUS WITHOUT KNOWING.` → `WHO THEY ALREADY ARE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?" In a world without refrigerators, salt was precious. It kept fish and meat from rotting. It brought out flavor. A little of it changed everything around it. But salt can lose its savor. Pure salt can't really stop being salt, but the salt people scraped from the Dead Sea or the marshes was mixed with other minerals. If the real salt washed out, what was left looked like salt and did nothing. Here's the scholar's detail: the Greek verb for lose its savor is moraino, from moros, foolish. It's where English gets moron. Salt that's lost its saltiness has literally become foolish. Then the second picture: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Picture a village on a Galilean hillside at night, its lamps glowing, visible for miles. Nobody, Jesus says, lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel basket. You put it on a stand so it lights the whole house. And then the line that ties it together: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Notice where the credit goes. Not so they see how good you are. So they glorify your Father. The light isn't a spotlight on you. It's a lamp that helps other people see. And notice the tense again. Not you should try to be light. Ye are.
screen: `SALT: KEEPS AND FLAVORS.` · `MORAINO: SALT GONE FOOLISH.` · `A CITY ON A HILL.` · `THE CREDIT GOES TO THE FATHER.` · then, large: `YE ARE THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one good work be seen. Settle, and breathe. Think of a small good thing you could do today that someone else would notice: helping a coworker in the open, thanking someone in front of others, holding a door and actually smiling. Not to be admired. Just to put a little light on the stand, so someone else can see by it. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can offer it to God ahead of time. The bell holds the time.
Salt and light. Two pictures of who Jesus's listeners already are: salt that keeps and flavors, and a light that can't be hidden.
Your line: you are the light. Today, do one good thing where it can be seen, and let the credit go past you. Day two hundred forty-one.

242.title: Not to abolish (Matthew 5:17–20)
242.hook: he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them
242.howItsDone: Christians read the Old Testament in worship alongside the Gospels, and many churches read a passage from the law or the prophets at every Sunday service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, salt and light, and your line was you are the light. Did you put one good thing on the stand? Day two hundred forty-two.

Some people picture Jesus as the one who came to throw out the old rulebook. Out with all those laws, in with love. It's a popular idea. And it's the very thing Jesus heads off in the next lines of the sermon. Remember who he's talking to: Jews on a hillside in Galilee, who had grown up with the Torah read aloud in the synagogue every Sabbath. They'd been wondering, maybe: is this new teacher against it? So before he says anything else, he answers.
screen: `THROW OUT THE OLD RULEBOOK?` → `A JEWISH CROWD IN GALILEE.` → `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, HE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil." The law here is the Torah, the first five books of the Bible, from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Torah is usually translated law, but the Hebrew word means more like teaching, or instruction: the way God shows people how to live. For Jews, it's the heart of scripture, and it still is. Then Jesus says: till heaven and earth pass, "one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled." A jot is the yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet, hardly bigger than an apostrophe. A tittle is a tiny stroke on a letter, the little hook that tells one Hebrew letter from another. Not even that much, he says, will be lost. So what does fulfill mean? Christians have understood it in several ways. Many say Jesus fulfills the law by living it completely, and by bringing out its deepest intent, which the rest of the chapter goes on to do. Many also say that parts of it, like the temple sacrifices, find their fulfillment in him. Churches differ on exactly how the law applies to Christians today, and Jews, for their part, continue to live by the Torah as their covenant with God. Then he says: unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. In his day the Pharisees were known for taking the law seriously, down to the details. He isn't lowering the bar. He's saying: go deeper, all the way to the heart.
screen: `TORAH: TEACHING, INSTRUCTION.` · `NOT ONE JOT OR TITTLE.` · `FULFILL: SEVERAL READINGS.` · `DEEPER, TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `NOT TO DESTROY, BUT TO FULFIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor your Jewish neighbors' scriptures. Settle, and breathe. The words Jesus is talking about are, first of all, the Torah, still read, sung and studied in synagogues every week. Think of a Jewish neighbor, friend or coworker, or of Jewish families you've never met, gathering around those same scrolls. Hold them in mind with respect and gratitude. If you pray, you can give thanks for the Torah and for the people who have carried it for three thousand years. The bell holds the time.
Torah. The first five books of the Bible; in Hebrew, not just law, but teaching: the way to live. Jesus says he came not to destroy it.
Your line: fulfill, not destroy. Today, when you're tempted to throw out something old, ask first what it was for, and whether you could carry it further. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: Anger (Matthew 5:21–26)
243.hook: before you bring your gift, go and be reconciled
243.howItsDone: In many churches the congregation shares the peace just before communion, a custom that echoes this passage, and some Christians make a point of mending quarrels before receiving communion or before Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Torah, and Jesus saying he came not to destroy but to fulfill. Did you ask what something old was for? Day two hundred forty-three.

Most of us have never killed anyone, and would feel pretty safe on that commandment. But most of us have muttered idiot at another driver. Most of us have rehearsed a furious speech in the shower, to someone who wasn't there. And most of us have walked into church, or a family dinner, or a meeting, while someone in the room was still upset with us, and just carried on. Yesterday Jesus said: go deeper, to the heart. Today he shows what that means, starting with one of the Ten Commandments.
screen: `NEVER KILLED ANYONE.` → `A FURIOUS SPEECH IN THE SHOWER.` → `DEEPER, TO THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, that it was said, thou shalt not kill. But I say unto you: whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of judgment. And whoever calls him raca, an Aramaic insult, roughly empty-head, is in danger too. This is the first of six times in this chapter Jesus says ye have heard, but I say unto you. He isn't canceling the commandment. He's following it back to its root. Murder starts somewhere: in contempt, in the name you call someone, in the grudge you feed. A small textual note: the King James says angry without a cause, but the oldest manuscripts don't have those words. Then Jesus tells a small, practical story. In the King James Bible: "Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Picture it. You've traveled to the temple in Jerusalem with an animal to offer. You're at the altar. It's the holiest moment of your year. And you remember that someone has something against you. Not that you're angry with them. That they're angry with you. Jesus says: leave the gift right there. Go. Make it right. Then come back. The Greek word is diallasso: to be changed toward someone, to be reconciled. In other words, the relationship with your neighbor isn't separate from your worship. Christians say God cares about both, and here the neighbor comes first.
screen: `YE HAVE HEARD, BUT I SAY.` · `RACA: EMPTY-HEAD.` · `LEAVE THY GIFT BEFORE THE ALTAR.` · `THEY HAVE SOMETHING AGAINST YOU.` · then, large: `FIRST BE RECONCILED TO THY BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reach out to someone you're angry with, or someone who's angry with you. Settle, and breathe. Let their face come to mind. Notice the anger, yours or theirs, without feeding it. You don't have to fix everything today. Just picture the first step: a message that says, can we talk? Or, I'm sorry for my part. If it isn't safe to reach out, simply let the anger rest for these two minutes. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Anger. Jesus follows thou shalt not kill back to its root, and says: before your gift, go and be reconciled.
Your line: reconcile first. Today, before one important thing you do, send one message that begins to mend something. Day two hundred forty-three.

244.title: The heart's look (Matthew 5:27–30)
244.hook: faithfulness starts in the eyes and the heart
244.howItsDone: Christians speak of guarding the heart and the eyes; in the Orthodox tradition this is called watchfulness, and many Christians examine what they've looked at and longed for in daily or weekly self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anger, and a gift left at the altar. Your line was reconcile first. Did you send a message that began to mend something? Day two hundred forty-four.

Every marriage, every friendship, every promise has a moment before the moment. Long before anyone does anything, there's a look that lingers. A daydream you keep returning to. A thought you feed instead of letting go. Nobody else can see it. It feels private and harmless. Yesterday Jesus followed thou shalt not kill back to anger. Today he does the same with another of the Ten Commandments, and follows it back to the eyes.
screen: `THE MOMENT BEFORE THE MOMENT.` → `A LOOK THAT LINGERS.` → `BACK TO THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard that it was said, thou shalt not commit adultery. And then, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." This isn't about noticing that someone is attractive. The Greek phrase means looking at someone in order to desire them: a look with a purpose, fed on purpose. And the verb for lust, epithumeo, is the same word the Greek Old Testament used in the last of the Ten Commandments: thou shalt not covet your neighbor's wife. So Jesus is joining two commandments together. The act and the wanting. The body and the heart. Faithfulness, he's saying, doesn't start at the door of a hotel room. It starts in what you let your eyes and your imagination rest on. Then comes one of his most startling images: if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away. If your right hand does, cut it off. Across the churches, Christians read this as vivid exaggeration, the way a teacher makes a point unforgettable, not as a literal instruction. What it means is: take this seriously. Be willing to cut off what feeds the wrong thing, whether that's an app, a habit, a late-night conversation, or a way of looking. And the same logic reaches far beyond marriage. Envy, greed, resentment all start the same way: with a look that lingers and gets fed. What you keep looking at, you start to want. What you want, you start to become.
screen: `YE HAVE HEARD: NO ADULTERY.` · `A LOOK WITH A PURPOSE.` · `EPITHUMEO: THE TENTH COMMANDMENT.` · `THE EYE AND THE HAND: TAKE IT SERIOUSLY.` · then, large: `ALREADY IN HIS HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard your eyes for one hour. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your eyes go when you're bored or tired: which feeds, which screens, which faces, which store windows. Notice one kind of looking that leaves you emptier, more envious or less faithful to someone. Now picture the next hour. Picture choosing to let your eyes rest somewhere else when that pull comes: the sky, a book, the person in front of you. If you pray, you can ask for a faithful heart. The bell holds the time.
The heart's look. Jesus traces unfaithfulness back from the act to the eyes and the heart: epithumeo, the look fed on purpose.
Your line: faithful in the heart. Today, for one hour, notice where your eyes go, and choose once to look away from something that feeds the wrong thing. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:33–37)
245.hook: no oaths needed if your word is plain
245.howItsDone: Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians affirm rather than swear in court, while many Christians take oaths in court or at ordination and try to keep ordinary promises as seriously as sworn ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart's look, and your line was faithful in the heart. Where did your eyes go, and did you choose once to look away? Day two hundred forty-five, the end of the week.

I swear. I promise. Honestly. To be fair. Trust me. Listen to how often people add a little booster to what they say, to make it count more. I swear I'll call you back. Honestly, I'm fine. And here's the odd thing: the more we use them, the more they suggest that without them, our words might not be true. If I have to say honestly, what was the rest? In the next lines of the sermon, Jesus takes on the biggest booster of his world: the oath.
screen: `I SWEAR. HONESTLY. TRUST ME.` → `WORDS WITH BOOSTERS.` → `THE BIGGEST BOOSTER: THE OATH.`

segments.voice: Ye have heard, he says, that you shall not break your oaths, but keep what you've sworn to the Lord. That was the law: if you swore by God, you had to keep it. But people had found loopholes. Swear by heaven, or by the earth, or by Jerusalem, or by your own head, and maybe it didn't count quite as much. Jesus closes every loophole. Heaven is God's throne. The earth is his footstool. Jerusalem is the city of the great King. You can't even make one hair of your head white or black. Everything you swear by belongs to God anyway. Then he says, in the King James Bible: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." The point isn't a new rule about courtrooms. It's that there shouldn't be two kinds of speech: sworn words you keep, and ordinary words you don't. If your yes always means yes, you never need to swear. The letter of James repeats it: let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay. Christians have lived this out in different ways. Quakers, Mennonites and some other Christians refuse to swear oaths at all, and affirm instead. That's one reason the United States Constitution lets a president swear or affirm. Many other Christians take oaths in court or in office, reading Jesus as teaching everyday honesty, not banning every oath. Both take the heart of it seriously: a plain word, kept. Look back at this week: peacemakers, the persecuted, salt and light, the Torah fulfilled, anger, the heart's look, and now a plain yes. Each goes deeper than the rule.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say only what you mean today. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Where did you say yes and mean maybe? Where did you say I'm fine and mean something else? Where did you add I swear or honestly? No guilt, just notice. Then picture today: one conversation where you'll say a plain yes or a plain no, and mean it. If you pray, you can ask for a plain, true tongue. The bell holds the time.
Let your yes be yes. Jesus closes the loopholes around oaths and asks for one kind of speech: yea, yea; nay, nay.
screen: `LET YOUR YES BE YES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: yes means yes. Today, drop the boosters. No I swear, no honestly. Just say what you mean, and do what you said. Day two hundred forty-five.

original.note: Greek: yes. the yea of Matthew 5:37; Greeks still say nai for yes today.

trapdoor: what you thought: this is a rule against swear words.
what it means: no loopholes; one kind of speech: a plain yes that means yes.
what a scholar hears: oaths by heaven, earth or Jerusalem were loopholes; Quakers and Anabaptists read it as a ban on oaths, others as a call to honesty.
